strengths: Addresses the important problem of test-time alignment for pre-trained discrete diffusion models without task-specific fine-tuning.
Combines twisted sequential Monte Carlo with an approximate locally optimal proposal and a first-order Taylor expansion to make reward-guided proposals tractable in discrete spaces.
Introduces a continuous relaxation of the carry-over unmasking constraint in masked diffusion models, enabling gradient-based proposal construction.
Provides a clear SMC framework and an algorithm that is straightforward to implement, with some promising results on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and binarized MNIST.
Includes appendices connecting the discrete-time formulation to continuous-time SMC and presenting additional experiments with ReMDM and UDLM.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is far too narrow for a top-tier AI conference: only a 2D mixture-of-Gaussians toy task and binarized MNIST are considered, despite the introduction claiming relevance to molecular generation, materials discovery, and math reasoning.

No comparisons are provided against relevant strong baselines such as fine-tuning/RL methods, discrete classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance, DDPP, or recent SMC-based discrete diffusion alignment methods. The approximate guidance baseline is weak and insufficient.

The central claim of being 'asymptotically unbiased' is not proven and is questionable in practice: the method uses an approximate first-order proposal, Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, and Monte Carlo estimated rewards, all of which introduce bias or approximation error without theoretical analysis.

Missing normalization constants and the handling of intractable twisting functions are not fully discussed; the locally optimal proposal is only approximated, and the resulting weight updates may not exactly target the intended reward-aligned distribution.
The novelty is incremental over existing SMC and guidance work for discrete diffusion. The main new components are engineering adaptations rather than a fundamentally new method.

The tempering schedule is hand-crafted and appears critical, especially for masked diffusion, but there is little systematic ablation over tempering, particle count, ESS threshold, resampling scheme, or Gumbel temperature.

MNIST results are mostly qualitative (visual samples); quantitative metrics such as reward, diversity, FID, or sample quality are not reported for the image experiments. The ReMDM and UDLM appendix experiments are also only visual.
Reproducibility is limited: no code, no full hyperparameter details for all experiments, no dataset splits, and no statistical significance or variance reporting across runs.
The paper overclaims relative to evidence: it uses small-scale experiments to support broad alignment claims and does not benchmark against the broader set of methods it discusses in related work.
Clarity and notation have issues, e.g., apparently malformed equations in the background section, and the distinction between exact and approximate SMC targets/proposals could be made much clearer.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: training-free test-time alignment for discrete diffusion models.
Combines twisted sequential Monte Carlo with an approximate locally optimal proposal and Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, making gradient-based guidance possible in discrete state spaces.
Provides a concrete algorithm and includes some theoretical discussion connecting the discrete-time SMC formulation to continuous-time SMC in the appendix.

Demonstrates on small synthetic and MNIST experiments that the proposed SMC approach can achieve higher reward and better diversity than naive reverse-process SMC or the approximate-guidance baseline.
Discusses limitations and briefly explores extensions to ReMDM and UDLM.
weaknesses: Evaluation is severely limited: only a 2D discretized mixture-of-Gaussians task and binarized MNIST, with no experiments on language, molecular design, math reasoning, or other domains mentioned in the introduction. This is far below the empirical standard for a top-tier AI conference.

No comparison to the closest prior work on SMC for discrete diffusion (Lee et al., 2025) or to standard discrete guidance/fine-tuning baselines such as D-CFG, D-CBG, or RL-based alignment methods. The main baseline, 'approximate guidance', is weak and derived from the same Taylor approximation.

The central claim of being 'asymptotically unbiased' is unsupported. The method uses an approximate proposal, Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, and Monte Carlo estimates of the reward; no convergence proof or pseudo-marginal treatment is given, and the target itself becomes noisy when the reward is estimated from samples.

Novelty is incremental. First-order Taylor approximations for guidance in discrete diffusion and twisted SMC for continuous diffusion already exist; the paper mainly combines these ideas with Gumbel-Softmax, without a substantial new theoretical or algorithmic contribution.

Technical issues undermine soundness: Eq. (18) appears to omit the normalizing constant of the proposal, reward gradients are evaluated on Gumbel-Softmax relaxed inputs that may be out-of-distribution for the reward model, and partial resampling is used without a clear correctness justification.

Experiments lack quantitative rigor: no FID, likelihood, classifier accuracy beyond reward, or statistical significance tests; MNIST results are primarily visual and only for a single target digit. Diversity in high-dimensional settings is not measured.

Scalability and reproducibility are unclear: key hyperparameters such as the Gumbel-Softmax temperature are not specified, no compute/time analysis is provided, and the tempering schedule is hand-tuned. The method is not shown to scale to realistic vocabularies or dimensions.

Clarity and presentation need improvement: notation is inconsistent, several equations are malformed or under-specified, and the CTMC appendix feels rushed and disconnected from the main empirical claims.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated approach: training-free test-time alignment for discrete diffusion via twisted SMC, avoiding task-specific fine-tuning.
Technically interesting adaptation: derives a first-order Taylor approximation of the locally optimal proposal and uses Gumbel-Softmax to enable gradient-based proposal updates in discrete spaces.
Addresses an important challenge in masked diffusion (immutable unmasked tokens) with a continuous formulation of the denoising output and provides gradient analysis.
Includes an algorithm, extended discussion of other discrete diffusion variants (ReMDM, UDLM), and a CTMC connection in the appendix.
Experiments on synthetic mixture-of-Gaussians and binarised MNIST show improvements over reverse-process proposal and approximate guidance in reward and diversity.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to simple synthetic mixture-of-Gaussians and binarised MNIST; no large-scale text, molecular, language, or reasoning tasks, making the broad claim of effectiveness insufficiently supported.

Baselines are weak and incomplete: only reverse process and approximate guidance are compared; missing comparisons to strong guidance methods (D-CBG, D-CFG), SMC-based discrete diffusion methods (e.g., Lee et al. 2025), and fine-tuning/RL baselines.

The claim of asymptotic unbiasedness is not rigorously justified under the proposed approximations (first-order Taylor expansion, Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, estimated reward), and the method likely targets an approximate distribution rather than the exact reward-aligned target.

Novelty is incremental: SMC/twisted SMC for diffusion and first-order Taylor approximations for guidance in discrete diffusion have appeared in prior work; the contribution is mainly an engineering combination for masked diffusion.
MNIST evaluation lacks quantitative metrics beyond reward and visual samples (e.g., classification accuracy, diversity, FID, calibration), and no error bars or multiple seeds are reported.

Key hyperparameters (tempering schedule, number of particles, Gumbel-Softmax temperature, ESS threshold, partial resampling details) appear hand-tuned and are not ablated; reproducibility is limited without code or detailed model/reward training specifications.
The paper relies heavily on appendix material for extended experiments and CTMC derivations, but the main text does not sufficiently establish significance for a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: Proposes a principled SMC framework for inference-time control of discrete diffusion models, with tractable importance weights for product and reward-tilting targets.

Derives locally optimal proposals and develops two practical approximations: a first-order gradient-based proposal and an amortised proposal trained by minimising the log-variance of importance weights.
Empirical results across synthetic tasks, language modelling, DNA design, and text-to-image generation demonstrate consistent improvements, often substantial (e.g., toxicity from 0.8% to 100%).
Provides extensive implementation details and hyperparameters, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the amortised proposal (Proposition 3) appears flawed: the proof claims the loss can be driven to zero, but Fψ(t) depends only on t and cannot absorb the x_t-dependent term log Z(x_t) - r(x_t) that remains even with the optimal proposal, undermining the claimed guarantee.

Ethical concerns are not adequately addressed: the language modelling experiment deliberately optimises for toxic text generation, producing 100% toxic samples, with only a superficial warning and no discussion of mitigation or safeguards.

Missing comparisons to existing test-time alignment methods (e.g., DRAKES), especially in language modelling and text-to-image tasks; baselines are limited to variants of the proposed method and simple BoN/CFG.
Some experimental results show trade-offs (e.g., reduced diversity or perplexity) that are noted but not deeply analysed, and hyperparameter sensitivity (λ_t, α) may limit practical adoption.
The paper contains several typographical errors (e.g., 'Sequence Monte Carlo', 'noising', inconsistent notation) that reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time control and scaling of discrete diffusion models, with potential applications in language, biology, and text-to-image generation.
Develops an SMC framework for discrete diffusion with tractable importance weights for product distributions and reward tilting, and connects it to continuous-time formulations.

Proposes practical proposal approximations (first-order gradient and amortised network) and demonstrates empirical gains across several domains, often improving reward alignment as the number of particles increases.
Provides supplementary proofs, implementation details, and additional experimental results in the appendix, showing awareness of reproducibility and practical implementation.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification for the amortised proposal appears flawed. Proposition 3 claims that minimising the per-step MSE loss L yields the locally optimal proposal and attains zero log-variance, but the log incremental weight under the locally optimal proposal generally depends on x_t through a state-dependent normalising constant. A time-only baseline Fψ(t) cannot absorb this dependence, so L=0 is not achievable in general. Thus the claimed link between L and L_log-var and the uniqueness/optimality claim are not established.

Much of the technical core is standard or already present in prior work: the locally optimal proposal is a classical SMC result, and Proposition 1 is explicitly noted to coincide with Holderrieth et al. (2025). The new contribution is mainly the amortised log-variance training objective, whose theoretical soundness is questionable.

Experimental evaluation is incomplete and sometimes unconvincing. For language modelling, the paper does not compare against recent discrete-diffusion SMC/alignment baselines such as Dang et al. (2025) or Singhal et al. (2025), and the toxicity results appear to exhibit reward hacking and substantial diversity degradation. For text-to-image generation, comparisons are limited to CFG and the proposed SMC variants, without clear baselines from alternative inference-time alignment or fine-tuning methods.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, the DNA design section reports mixed results against DRAKES but characterises the remaining metrics as comparable or favourable; the language modelling section downplays a significant drop in Dist-3 (e.g., 90 vs. 96) despite claiming sample quality is largely preserved.

Clarity and presentation need substantial improvement: numerous typographical and notation errors (e.g., “nosing”, “Sequence Monte Carlo”, inconsistent use of x_s/x_{t-1}, α and λ, unclear equations), undefined assumptions, and derivations that are difficult to follow. This makes the technical content harder to verify and reduces confidence in the theoretical claims.

Ethical concerns are not adequately addressed. The language modelling experiment intentionally optimises a toxicity classifier and produces highly toxic text; while a warning is included, the paper does not discuss mitigation, dual-use risks, or safeguards beyond the research illustration.

strengths: Proposes a principled SMC framework for discrete diffusion models with tractable importance weights for product and reward-tilting targets, addressing an important test-time alignment problem.

Provides theoretical characterization of the locally optimal proposal and a log-variance minimization objective, with Corollary 1 and Proposition 3 offering uniqueness and an upper bound connecting the practical objective to log-variance reduction.
Develops two practical approximations—gradient-based and amortized proposals—and demonstrates that better proposal approximation consistently improves SMC performance across particle counts.

Broad empirical evaluation spans synthetic MoG/MNIST, language modelling, DNA design, and text-to-image generation, with consistent gains over pretrained, BoN, and SMC_base baselines, including scaling with number of particles.
weaknesses: The importance weights rely on a detailed-balance approximation pθ(x_{t-1})/pθ(x_t) ≈ pθ(x_{t-1}|x_t)/p(x_t|x_{t-1}); the paper does not quantify the resulting bias, and the claim that reward-tilting eliminates this error is overstated because the approximation remains unless the learned reverse model equals the true data score.

The amortised proposal requires reward-based training, so the method is not purely inference-time; comparisons to relevant fine-tuning/test-time alignment baselines (e.g., DRAKES in language, RL/DPOK-style methods in text-to-image, or exact Singhal et al. SMC) are limited or missing, weakening empirical positioning.

Several technical and presentation issues remain: inconsistency in product-target weight normalisation (Eq. 6 vs. remark in A.1), unclear handling of the λ_t schedule in importance weights, minor typos (e.g., 'Multinormial'), and Algorithm 1/2 notation could be clearer.

Diversity/quality trade-offs are not fully resolved: SMC_amot often reduces diversity/perplexity (e.g., Dist and PPL in language; 3-mer/JASPAR in DNA), and the paper does not deeply analyse when this trade-off is acceptable or how to control it.

Reproducibility and cost: no code release is mentioned, and the computational overhead of training the amortised proposal and running SMC with many particles is not systematically reported, making practical scalability harder to assess.
